question: Your developer productivity agent connects to three MCP servers. Through the deploy server's deploy_service tool it can release code, but policy says that each production release must go to an on-call engineer for approval instead. The ticket server returns dates as Unix timestamps and the CI server returns ISO 8601 strings, so the agent often puts events in the wrong order. Which hook design meets both needs?

options.text: Intercept outgoing deploy_service calls to block production releases and route them to on-call approval, and intercept outgoing ticket and CI tool calls to normalize the dates.
options.reason: Interception of outgoing calls acts before the tools return any data, so it cannot normalize the date formats in the results; that is the job of a PostToolUse hook.

options.text: Intercept outgoing deploy_service calls to block production releases and route them to on-call approval, and use a PostToolUse hook to normalize the dates.
options.reason: A tool call interception hook stops the release before it runs and redirects it to approval, and a PostToolUse hook transforms tool results before the agent processes them.

options.text: Add a PostToolUse hook on deploy_service results that blocks production releases and routes them to on-call approval, and another PostToolUse hook that normalizes the dates.
options.reason: A PostToolUse hook sees deploy_service only after the call has run, so the production release has already happened when the hook acts.

options.text: Use a PostToolUse hook to normalize the dates, and add a system prompt rule that the agent must request on-call approval before each production release.
options.reason: A prompt rule gives only probabilistic compliance, so the agent may still release to production in some runs; a hook is needed for a guaranteed block.
